conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you could come in today. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks and months after birth. What we’re about to do is a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s 10 gentle questions that help us see how you’ve been coping emotionally over the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting—just a temperature check on your mood and anxiety. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else, and then we talk together about the safest next steps. We’ll go through the questions one by one, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to begin?

**1.** In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not very much. I’ll chuckle if my husband makes a joke or if the baby does something cute, but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time I’m too tired or just down to really find things funny the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I manage a little laugh when my husband jokes around or when the baby makes a silly face, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too tired or just down to really find things funny the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still try to plan little things—like a walk with the stroller or grabbing coffee—but when the time comes I just feel “meh.” It’s like the excitement drains out before I even get there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong—like I’m already failing him. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to an appointment, turns into “I’m a bad mom” in my head.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps racing—Is he breathing? Is the room too cold? Am I holding him right? I’ll check the monitor a dozen times even though I know he’s fine. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but the worries just pop back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a few times—maybe twice this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, heart’s racing, and I feel like something awful is about to happen even though there’s no real reason. It passes if I pace the hallway or do the breathing the nurse showed me, but in the moment it’s scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to sleep, it all piles up. I’ll look at the dirty dishes or the laundry mountain and think, “I can’t do this,” but somehow I still push through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week, yeah. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—thinking I’m doing everything wrong, worrying something will happen to the baby—and then I’m wide-awake for ages. When I finally nod off, I still wake up once or twice with those anxious thoughts and have to stare at the ceiling until they fade.
I have felt sad or miserable
Most of the time, really. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I still smile for the baby and try to keep going, but underneath I just feel… sad.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve broken down a couple of times this week. Once was after I couldn’t get him to latch—just sat there in the rocker bawling because it felt like one more thing I’m failing at. The other time was when my mom pointed out I hadn’t showered in three days; I laughed at first, then the tears just started coming and I couldn’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Um… it has flashed through my mind, maybe once or twice, when everything feels too heavy. Nothing planned—just this quick, scary “what if I weren’t here” thought, and then I feel awful for even thinking it. I push it away and focus on the baby, but it keeps popping back in.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy, with joy seeming out of reach, constant worries about your baby, and moments of tearfulness and self-doubt. It's understandable to feel overwhelmed after birth, yet your description of persistent low mood, intrusive worries, and fleeting thoughts of not wanting to be here tells us you deserve extra support right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports only occasional, forced laughter—clearly less than before—matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient still attempts to plan activities but reports markedly reduced enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive self-blame for routine parenting challenges, indicating "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily racing worries about the baby with compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes clear panic episodes happening twice this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and unable to manage tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes clear sleep disruption several nights this week linked to unhappiness/anxiety, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states feeling sad 'most of the time' and describes pervasive low mood despite efforts to function.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes this week triggered by feelings of failure, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of self-harm that are distressing but not planned, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 places you well above the EPDS threshold of 14 that flags probable major depression. You endorse <sym>sad mood</sym>, markedly reduced <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>excessive self-blame</sym>, <sym>daily anxiety</sym> with compulsive checking, <sym>panic attacks</sym>, <sym>insomnia</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym>. These findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Positive response on Item 10 signals elevated safety risk requiring immediate clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental health team</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you until professional support is in place; share your thoughts so you are not alone with them
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or 911 if thoughts of self-harm escalate or you feel unsafe
4. Consider starting evidence-based treatment options your provider may discuss, such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med>
5. Practice small self-care steps: accept help with housework, aim for a 20-minute stroller walk outdoors, and give yourself permission to rest when baby sleeps
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screen – Structured Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report via 10-item questionnaire (Edinburgh format)

Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, crying spells nearly daily  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation for previously pleasant activities  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding parenting performance  
- Chronic worry, intrusive “what-if” thoughts, nightly monitor-checking  
- Two discrete panic episodes this week (chest tightness, racing heart)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by ruminative worry  
- Frequent feeling “overwhelmed,” unable to manage routine tasks  
- Passive suicidal ideation (transient, no plan, no intent); thoughts of “not wanting to be here” ×2 in past week

Risk Factors Identified  
1. Depressed mood plus loss of pleasure ≥2 wk duration  
2. Anxiety symptoms meeting clinical threshold (daily worry, panic attacks)  
3. Sleep disruption directly linked to mood/anxiety  
4. Excessive maternal guilt / cognitions of inadequacy  
5. Passive self-harm ideation → elevated safety concern

Screening Impression  
Responses indicate moderate-to-high likelihood of postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features. Passive suicidal ideation present; safety assessment warranted. Recommend prompt formal evaluation by perinatal mental-health specialist and same-day safety planning.
